title: AI Coding Agents Should Make Migrations Easier. Without Context, They Make Them Worse.
summary: You have to understand the legacy system before you can safely change it. That understanding is exactly what agents lack.
body_text: AI Coding Agents Should Make Migrations Easier. Without Context, They Make Them Worse. You have to understand the legacy system before you can safely change it. That understanding is exactly what agents lack. Apr 20, 2026 — 5 min read Adam Co-founder Share on X Share on LinkedIn Share on Facebook A consultancy we work with was evaluating a 3 to 4 million line legacy .NET codebase for a potential modernization engagement. ASP.NET Web Forms, Entity Framework, built over five to seven years by a team they’d never met. Their lead’s assessment: “Who knows what’s in there? We don’t have a lot of folks today that are familiar with ASP.NET Web Forms. This is legacy. We just don’t operate in this environment anymore.” Before committing 12 people to a multi-month engagement, they wanted to understand what they were getting into. “I’d rather spend a couple thousand dollars figuring that out over three, four weeks before we invest in it and put our reputation on the line.” This is the migration problem in its purest form. Before you can change a system, you have to understand it. And understanding a large, old codebase is exactly the kind of work that AI coding tools should excel at. But in practice, it’s where they fail most spectacularly. The Migration Paradox Migrations are the highest-leverage use case for AI coding agents. Rewriting legacy code, updating frameworks, decomposing monoliths, moving between platforms. These are the projects where engineering teams spend months on work that feels mechanical, where AI should provide the most acceleration. The paradox: migrations are also where agents need the most context and have the least. The legacy system is the thing nobody fully understands. That’s why you’re migrating in the first place. Documentation is years out of date. The engineers who built it have moved on. The code has accumulated multiple implementations of the same patterns, workarounds layered on workarounds, and implicit contracts that nobody documented. A CIO at a fintech with an 8 million line Ruby monolith described it: “There’s metaprogramming, monkey patching, all these things. You have to know where those skeletons are buried. We haven’t done a great job pruning or consolidating. Over the years we’ve had three implementations trying to address the same problem, and we haven’t been consistent in saying from this point forward, only use implementation three.” That’s the system the agent has to understand before it can safely change anything. What Happens When You Skip the Understanding One of our customers learned this the hard way. They were running a 12-week modernization project on a 10 million line legacy Java ERP. Early in the project, they adopted Claude Code without any context infrastructure in place. The agents were productive. They wrote code. They made changes. The problem: the changes created additional technical debt. The agents went down rabbit holes, made modifications based on incomplete understanding, and introduced inconsistencies. The team had to clean up after the agents. The project was stuck for over 9 months. A consultant working on the project described how they tried to build understanding without pre-computed context: “Four of us, we all did the same thing on the same code with Claude and generated markdown files. Started to share them about and read through. When we all felt confident they were right, that’s when we gained confidence.” Four developers independently generating docs from an AI, cross-checking them against each other, then validating with the client team. And still finding errors. After adding Driver’s pre-computed codebase context, the trajectory changed. Sessions ran longer without going off track. Their testing workflow produced reliable results. In their words, they went from “utterly broken, hit a wall” to “light at the end of the tunnel.” The consultant leading the engagement at a private equity firm that funded the project put it bluntly: Claude “has no chance” on 10 million lines of code without pre-computed context. Five Kinds of Migration, Same Problem We see migrations across our customers in several forms, and the underlying challenge is always the same: you need to understand the existing system deeply before you can change it. Language and platform migrations. Moving from one language or framework to another. The 10 million line Java ERP being modernized. A fintech pivoting from a Ruby monolith to Python and TypeScript microservices. In both cases, the agent needs to understand the old system’s patterns, contracts, and dependencies before it can produce equivalent implementations in the new stack. Infrastructure and tooling migrations. Changing source control, CI/CD, or deployment platforms. One customer migrated from Azure DevOps to GitHub. Commits transferred, but PRs didn’t. Their pipelines were still in Azure DevOps. The migration split their development history across two systems, and the context about why changes were made was partially lost. Architecture migrations. Decomposing a monolith into services, or consolidating fragmented services. The fintech CIO described engineers who “didn’t grow up with this codebase” feeling trepidation about working in the monolith. New engineers build new services in Python. Legacy engineers maintain the Ruby monolith. Nobody wants to be the person who breaks the old system. Compliance modernization. A defense contractor with a 20+ year C++ codebase needs to retroactively extract software requirements from existing code to align with V-model standards. Not a code migration, but the same deep understanding requirement. Their director of software said: “We’ve seen tools work great on small codebases and tail off at scale. A million lines of code is where things break.” Due diligence. Consultancies and companies evaluating acquisitions or vendor transitions need to understand a codebase before committing resources. The consultancy we opened with treats this as an “insurance policy.” A few thousand dollars and a few weeks of investigation before signing a deal that puts their reputation on the line. What Migration Requires From Context Every migration scenario requires the same four things from codebase context: Exhaustive understanding of the existing system. Not samples. Not search results. Complete, structured knowledge of every symbol, every dependency, every pattern in the legacy code. Automatic currency. The legacy system is still under active development during the migration. Context that’s a week old is already wrong. Structural awareness. Not just what code exists, but how it’s connected. Call graphs, dependency trees, implicit contracts between modules. RAG-based approaches destroy this structural information by chunking code into text fragments. Cross-codebase visibility. Migrations almost always span multiple repos. The monolith, the new services, the shared libraries, the infrastructure configuration. An agent working on the migration needs to see all of it. We’ve written about why current approaches to context fail at delivering these properties and why we built a compiler instead of a search engine to solve them. For migrations specifically, the compiler approach means the agent starts every session with a complete, current, structured map of the legacy system. It doesn’t have to rediscover the architecture. It can focus on the actual migration work. Archaeology Into Engineering Migrations have always been expensive because understanding the legacy system was manual work. You assigned senior engineers to read code, trace dependencies, and document what they found. That understanding was perishable: stale the moment someone pushed a commit. And it was trapped in the heads of the people who did the investigation. Pre-computed codebase context changes the economics. The understanding is exhaustive, automatically current, and available to every engineer and agent working on the migration. The archaeology becomes engineering. If you’re planning a migration and wondering whether AI coding tools will help or create more problems, the answer depends entirely on context.

title: Changing Your Job Title on a Resume: Reframing vs. Lying
summary: You can translate a quirky or underselling job title into its truthful industry-standard equivalent. You cannot invent a level you never held. Here is the line.
body_text: Can you change your job title on a resume? Yes, within one clear limit. You can translate a title into its truthful industry-standard equivalent, so a "Customer Happiness Ninja" becomes a "Customer Success Representative" and a recruiter and their software both understand it. You can also clarify a title that undersold what you actually did. What you cannot do is promote yourself to a level you never held or invent a role your employer never gave you. The working test is simple: would your old manager and HR confirm this title without hesitating? If yes, it is a reframe. If they would raise an eyebrow, it is a lie, and lies get caught during verification. Your last company called you a "Digital Overlord." Or a "Marketing Guru." Or maybe it did something quieter and worse: it hired you as an "intern," kept you for three years, handed you a real analyst's workload, and never once updated the title. Now you are staring at that string of words on your resume, and it either sounds like a joke or it sounds like a job you have long since outgrown. So you wonder if you can just change it. The honest answer, from the recruiting side of the table, is that there is a line here and it is sharper than most advice admits. Translation sits on one side of it, and it is usually the smart move. Fabrication sits on the other, a slow-motion landmine that tends to go off at the worst possible moment. This piece is about finding that line and staying on the safe side of it, without leaving good work buried under a title nobody can decode. One thing up front so we do not talk past each other. This is not about the headline at the top of your resume, the "Senior Software Engineer | Cloud Architect" line under your name, which is a separate thing with its own resume-title guide . Here we mean the actual job title you held at a past employer, the one sitting next to the company name in your work history, and how much freedom you have to change it. The line: translation versus fabrication Hold onto one distinction and most of the confusion disappears. Choosing how to describe a real job is editing; inventing a job is lying. They feel similar in the moment, since both involve typing something other than the exact string HR filed away, but a recruiter treats them as opposite categories, and so should you. Translation means taking the true nature of what you did and expressing it in the language the market uses. Your employer's internal name for the role was odd, or vague, or a running joke, so you swap it for the standard equivalent that means the same thing. You still did that job. You are just saying so in words a stranger can parse. Fabrication means claiming a level, a scope, or a role you did not have. You were a coordinator and you write "Manager" even though you managed nobody and controlled no budget. You were out of work and you invent a consulting gig. You bump yourself from mid-level to senior because the posting asks for senior. Nothing you did changed; only the claim did, and the claim is now false. Here is the test that decides which one you are doing, and it takes about five seconds. Picture your old manager and the HR person who processed your paychecks, sitting across from your prospective employer, being asked "did this person hold this title and do this work?" If both would say yes without flinching, you have translated. If either would hesitate, correct the record, or say "well, not exactly," you have crossed into fabrication. That imagined confirmation is not hypothetical, by the way. It is roughly what a background check does, which is why the test works. Why a quirky or non-standard title is a real problem Cute internal titles are not just embarrassing; they cost you real money, and they do it at two different stages of the process. The software stage comes first. Before any human reads your resume, an applicant tracking system parses it and tries to match your history against the open role, hunting for the standard vocabulary of the job, terms like "Customer Success," "Software Engineer," "Account Executive." A field that says "Customer Happiness Ninja" carries no keyword the parser recognizes, so the four years of relevant work sitting behind it can register as a blank the machine never scores. The human stage is where it gets worse. A recruiter working through forty resumes before lunch has to sort each one in a few seconds, and a title they cannot decode is friction at exactly the wrong moment. Nobody emails you to ask what a "Wizard of Engineering" did all day; they flip to the next candidate whose history reads cleanly. And the deliberately goofy swing, the person who lists "Jedi Knight" to stand out, lands even worse. Campus recruiters and career-services reviewers are blunt about that move: the resume tends to go straight in the bin, a standing example of what not to do. So a quirky title is not a personality flex. It is a comprehension gap wedged between your real experience and the person deciding whether to pick up the phone, and translating it into a term people recognize is just closing that gap. The translation playbook: find the market-standard equivalent Translating a title well is a small, disciplined exercise, and the discipline is the whole point. You are not fishing for the most impressive words you can get away with. You are hunting for the true ones the market has already settled on for the job you did. Figuring that out is easier than it sounds. Pull up three or four job postings for the work you actually performed and watch what those roles are called. The company that hired you as a "Growth Hacker" was, nine times out of ten, hiring for what everyone else calls a Digital Marketing Specialist, or a Marketing Manager if your scope was wider. "People Operations Partner" almost always maps to HR Generalist. A "Solutions Evangelist" is usually a Sales Engineer wearing a costume. The equivalent already exists in plain language, and you are just calling it by that name. Then run it past your real level before you commit. The standard term has to fit not only what you did but how senior you were when you did it. A "Digital Overlord" who single-handedly built and maintained the company website is a Web Developer, full stop, not a Director of Engineering. Get both the function and the level honest and you have not bent a single rule. If you want a belt-and-suspenders version, show both. Some people list the standard equivalent as the main title and keep the official one in parentheses, so the resume reads "Customer Success Representative (internal title: Customer Happiness Hero)." That hands the recruiter the recognizable term and the verifiable one at the same time, and it removes any question about whether you changed anything. It reads a little clunky, so save it for genuinely bizarre internal titles or roles where verification runs strict. For most quirky titles, a clean standard translation on the resume plus the correct official title on the background-check form is enough. One rule underneath all of this: the standard title you choose still has to describe you accurately. Swapping "Ninja" for "Representative" is translation. Swapping "Representative" for "Manager" because it sounds better is not, and no amount of "but titles are meaningless" talk changes that. The words are only meaningless until someone verifies them. When your title undersold you: clarifying scope without inventing it The opposite problem is more common than the goofy-title one, and it is where reframing does the most honest good. Your title understated what you did. You were an "Associate" who quietly ran a team. You were hired as an "intern" and never got re-titled even after you took on a full workload. You were a "Developer" who was doing the tech lead's job because the company handed you the responsibilities and skipped the promotion, which happens so often it has a name now, the dry promotion. Underselling is not harmless either, because a title sorts you for the future as much as it records the past. Recruiters filling a mid-level or senior req filter partly on the titles already sitting in your history. A label that reads two rungs below where you actually worked can drop your resume in the wrong pile before anyone reaches the accomplishments that would have corrected it. For anyone trying to climb, that understated title is a quiet tax you pay on every application. The fix is to let the resume reflect the work, with a light touch. Lots of companies run a formal title in the HR system and a functional one everyone actually uses out loud, and that functional working title is fair game; if the "Developer" in payroll was the "Tech Lead" in every standup, list Tech Lead. Where the honest label for your scope sits one notch above your filed title, and your manager would back you up on that scope, clarify it with a parenthetical that keeps the official version visible, so the line reads "Marketing Coordinator (Team Lead)" or "Support Associate (acting Support Lead)." Written that way it tells the truth twice over, which is exactly what you want a verification check to find. The trap here is treating "I did more than my title" as a blank check to invent a level. Covering a tech lead's tasks for a quarter is real, and it earns a clarification. Writing "Engineering Manager" when you never had a single report, a dollar of budget, or the authority the word implies is a different thing entirely, and interviewers smell it fast. What keeps a scope clarification honest is that it stays roped to work you genuinely did; cut that rope and the clarification becomes fabrication in a helpful costume. And the rope, in practice, is your bullets, which is why they matter more than the title line ever will. Let your bullets carry the truth, not the title Ask enough recruiters and hiring managers and you hear the same line, which takes most of the air out of the title panic: they read the responsibilities before they trust the label. The title tells them roughly where to file you. The three or four bullets under it tell them who you really are. Whichever way your title is off, the work described below it corrects the record, whether that means pulling an inflated label back down to earth or lifting a modest one up to where you actually operated. So lean on the bullets rather than the title line. Tempted to bump "Support Associate" up to "Support Lead"? Leave the title alone and write the three bullets that make the case for you: resolved the queue's ugliest escalations, trained two new hires, owned the team's response-time number. A recruiter reads that and thinks "lead" on their own, and you never had to type a word you would sweat over during verification. Strong, specific, verb-led bullets carry the whole load here; if yours read thin, a couple of our resources on writing resume achievements and choosing action words and power verbs are worth a pass, and the guide to showing P&L or budget responsibility earns its keep when the scope you are claiming is financial. Catch yourself wanting to stretch a title, and nine times out of ten there is a stronger bullet sitting right there unused. Not sure your title reframe reads clean? Run your resume through a free review and see whether a recruiter and the parser would understand your titles the way you intend them, before you send it out. Get a free resume review → The danger zone: inflating your title Now the move to skip. Bumping "Coordinator" up to "Manager," or bolting "Senior" onto a role that never earned it. It feels low-stakes, because it is one word and everyone keeps repeating that titles are made up anyway. Sure. Titles are fuzzy, and one word is small. That still will not save you, because the word is checkable and the check tends to land at the worst possible time. Walk the sequence. You inflate the title. The interviews go well. You get the offer, accept it, give notice at your current job. The relief lasts about a week. Then the verification runs, the report reads "Coordinator" where your resume said "Manager," and the conversation you are suddenly in is about whether you lie on documents, not whether you can do the work. Your old seat is already being backfilled. That is the trap, and it springs right after you have kicked away the ledge. The interview can blow it up even earlier, before any report exists. Say "Manager" out loud and a decent interviewer gets curious. How big was the team? Walk me through a performance conversation you had to have. What did you actually own of the budget? If the real answers are nobody, never, and nothing, you are stuck choosing between a fresh lie and watching your own claim fold in real time. Interviewers have sat across from enough puffed-up titles to recognize the shape of it: the resume announces one level, the follow-up answers admit a quieter one, and that distance carries further than a modest title ever would have. What verification actually catches It pays to know exactly what one of these checks confirms, because the truth sits between two loud and wrong camps. The panic camp thinks screeners audit everything you have ever done. The "they never check" camp swears it is all criminal history and nobody looks at titles. Reality lands in the middle, and both camps will lead you to a bad decision. A standard employment-verification check nails down three facts about each past job: the employer, your dates, and your title. It gets them one of two ways. Sometimes the screening company phones your former employer's HR directly. More often these days, it pulls the record from an automated service, the biggest being The Work Number, run by Equifax, which corporate payroll systems feed on a set schedule. Whatever title your old employer's payroll reported flows into that database and can come back on the report next to your dates, refreshed every pay cycle you were there. The screening vendors most companies hire query these sources as a matter of routine, not as a special deep dive. So the honest picture is this. Many entry-level and mid-level checks are light and focused on criminal history, and plenty of people with small title tweaks never hear a thing. But title and dates are exactly what a standard verification is built to confirm, senior and regulated roles almost always run the thorough version, and you cannot tell from the outside which kind a given employer will order. Betting they will not look is a bet you place with your accepted offer as the stake. Here is the reassuring wrinkle, and it is the reframe-versus-lie split showing up on paper. A truthful translation that happens to mismatch a stale HR record is extremely common and usually harmless. It is routine for a check to come back listing someone as a "Business Development Representative" when they had run operations for years, simply because nobody updated the payroll system as their pay and duties climbed, and employers shrug that off all the time. When a report flags that kind of gap, it usually lands as a "consider" or "discrepancy" status rather than an instant no, and a short explanation or an old paystub clears it. What sinks a candidacy is a material misrepresentation, the kind you cannot explain in one honest sentence. That is the exact line the screener draws, and it is the same line this whole piece is about. For the full picture of what these checks do and do not surface, our breakdown of what a background check actually shows goes deeper, and how long a background check takes covers the timeline. Keep the story consistent across resume, LinkedIn, and references Whatever title you land on, it cannot live only on your resume. It has to survive contact with the two other places an employer looks: your LinkedIn and your references. A resume that says "Marketing Coordinator," a LinkedIn that still says "Intern," and a former manager who describes you as "our analyst" is three different stories, and three stories about one job is exactly the kind of noise that makes a careful employer nervous. So get all three saying the same thing. Translate your title the same way on LinkedIn that you did on the resume. If your reframe leans on a working title or a scope your old manager would vouch for, give that manager a heads-up before you list them, so the reference call and the resume match instead of colliding. None of this is coaching you to lie, quite the reverse. The whole reason to keep the story consistent is that the story is true, and a true account repeated the same way across three sources reads as solid, while the same truth told three slightly different ways still plants a doubt you did not need to plant. That reference call doubles as a useful gut check. If matching your resume title to what your old boss will actually say means you have to warn them not to contradict you, the warning itself is the tell that you have drifted from translation into fabrication, and it is announcing the problem before any employer gets there. The test is whether your old manager, describing the job in their own words, would land somewhere near the title you wrote, and if they would, the call quietly confirms you rather than catching you out. What to say if the discrepancy comes up Say you translated an honestly weird internal title and, because HR never updated its system, the verification came back with the original oddball string. This is the good version of a discrepancy, and it has a calm, one-sentence answer. Something like: "My company used non-standard internal names for standard roles, so I listed the industry-standard equivalent to make my experience clear. Happy to share my offer letter or a paystub." Delivered evenly, that resolves it, because it is true and it is reasonable. That sentence lands because it is not a defense at all, just a plain description of what you did and why you labeled it the way you did, and plain descriptions hold up when someone asks a follow-up. Now try writing the equivalent sentence for an inflated title. Go ahead, take a swing at turning "I wrote Manager but managed nobody" into a reasonable choice. There is no honest version, which is why people in that spot end up scrambling instead of answering. Here is the tell worth watching for in yourself: the day you are rehearsing a story built to survive scrutiny instead of simply recounting what happened, the thing that needs fixing is the resume, not the rehearsal. Keep a light paper trail for the honest version, just in case. An offer letter, an old paystub, or an email showing your working title makes a translated title trivial to back up if anyone ever asks, and most of the time nobody does. That is not you covering tracks. It is you making it costless to prove you did something right, which closes the topic on the spot. When to just keep the official title as-is Reframing is a tool, not an assignment. A lot of the time the smart move is to leave your title exactly as your employer wrote it. When the official version already reads as a clean, recognizable term, "Staff Accountant" or "Project Manager" and the like, do not lay a finger on it; rewording a title that was fine only plants a needless mismatch with your verification record and buys you nothing. A narrower set of titles carries legal or credential weight, and those are not yours to reword at all. A Registered Nurse earned that label from a state board and an exam, not from whoever signs the payroll. Same story for a CPA, a Professional Engineer, an attorney admitted to the bar. Round "Paralegal" up to "Attorney" or "Bookkeeper" up to "CPA" and you have not translated anything; you have misstated a credential, which bites in a way the goofy-title cases never will. Think of the Walmart communications executive who resigned in 2014 when a background re-check during a promotion surfaced a college degree he had never actually finished, eight years into the job. Credentialed claims get verified again and again, sometimes years after you assumed the question was buried, so in medicine, law, finance, and engineering, precision on your title is plain self-preservation. And when your company inflated your title but you cannot honestly translate it down without underselling your real scope, the cleanest answer is often to keep the official title and let a parenthetical or the bullets carry the context. Stuck between choices, fall back on your true official title plus strong bullets that show the work. That pairing is honest, it survives verification, and it usually persuades hard enough that the title line stops carrying the weight you feared it did. The same principle, applied everywhere on your resume Zoom out and the title question is really one case of a rule that runs the whole resume: you get to choose how you present true things, and you never get to dress false things up as true. Drop the ancient irrelevant jobs, lead with your strengths, group your experience so it reads clean, translate jargon a stranger would not follow, all fair game. Inventing is the one move that is off the table, and that line does not move an inch whether the subject is your title, your dates, or your seniority. We have written this exact line in a couple of other places because it keeps coming up. The honest way to handle a career gap runs on the same distinction applied to your dates: you can frame a gap plainly, but you cannot fudge the dates around it, because the same verification that checks your title checks your timeline. Whether to downplay an overqualified background is the reframe-versus-lie boundary applied to your seniority, where you can omit a credential that makes you a flight risk but cannot claim a level you never reached. Learn the line once for your title and you have learned it for the whole document. If your applications are stalling and you are not sure the title is even the issue, it usually is not the biggest one. Our teardown of why resumes actually get rejected walks through the flaws that cost you more, and the full map of how hiring actually works shows where a title matters and where it stops mattering. Get the title clear, get the rest of the resume right, and this small anxious question can go back to being small. Frequently Asked Questions Is it lying to change my job title on my resume? Not if you are translating, and yes if you are inventing. Turning "Customer Happiness Ninja" into "Customer Success Representative" just describes the same real job in words people recognize, which is honest. Turning "Coordinator" into "Manager" when you managed nobody claims a rung you never stood on, which is not. The quick gut check is whether your old boss and HR could confirm what you wrote without reaching for a correction. When the answer is yes, you translated; the moment they would push back, you have wandered into inventing. Will a background check catch a changed job title? It can, because a standard employment check confirms your employer, dates, and title, either by calling your old HR or pulling the record from a service like The Work Number. So a fabricated title that contradicts the record will surface. Here is the nuance that saves honest people: a truthful translation that mismatches a stale HR entry usually comes back as a "consider" flag, not a rejection, and one calm sentence plus a paystub clears it. A material lie is the one that gets an offer pulled. Can I put a title I never officially had if I did the work? You can clarify the scope you genuinely operated at, but you cannot manufacture a level you never reached. An "Associate" who really did lead a team can fairly write "Marketing Coordinator (Team Lead)," the kind of clarification a manager would back up on a reference call. A coordinator who just wants to sound like a manager, with no reports and no authority behind the word, is not clarifying anything; that is invention with better marketing. What decides it is always whether the underlying work supports the claim, never whether the claim reads more impressively. My title was an internal joke like "Marketing Guru." What do I use instead? Use the standard term for what you did. Read a few postings for that work and copy the vocabulary they use: a marketing "guru" is usually a Marketing Specialist or Marketing Manager depending on how much you owned. If the internal title was truly bizarre, list the standard one and put the official one in parentheses so the recruiter gets the recognizable label and the verifiable one at once. On the background-check form, though, always enter the real official title your employer has on file. Do recruiters and ATS software actually care about the exact title? Yes, though the two care about completely different things. The software is scanning for standard keywords, so a non-standard title can render your relevant experience invisible to the parser no matter how good the work was. A human is not reading the words that closely; they are trying to file you fast, and a title they cannot decode is friction that quietly slides a resume into the maybe-later pile. One clear, standard title handles both worries in a single stroke. An inflated one handles neither, earning zero extra credit from the parser and getting caught by the interviewer the minute the scope questions start. What if my LinkedIn title doesn't match my resume? Fix it so they match. Employers pull up both, and a resume saying "Marketing Coordinator" over a LinkedIn still frozen at "Intern" plants a doubt you never needed. Whatever translation you used on the resume, carry it over to LinkedIn word for word, and make sure your references would describe you the same way. You are aiming for one account of the job that holds steady across all three sources, because the same true story wobbling from place to place reads as shifty even when every version of it is accurate. Is it OK to change "Junior Developer" to just "Developer"? Usually yes, if you were doing the full role and not a trainee's slice of it. Companies hand out "Junior" and "Senior" so inconsistently that the words barely mean anything across employers. Shedding a "Junior" you outgrew two years ago? Mild, defensible, nobody blinks. Adding a "Senior" you never earned is the move that bites, because it is exactly what an interviewer digs into when the scope questions start. Match the label to the work you did. Plain developer, then "Developer." Operating like a senior, then prove it in the bullets and let the title follow. My company never gave me a formal title. What do I put? Give yourself the standard title that honestly describes the work. Small companies skip titles constantly, so you are not fabricating anything by naming the role yourself. Ran the office day to day? "Office Manager." Spent your time coordinating operations? "Operations Coordinator." Both describe reality; neither invents a rank. Just keep it pinned to the level you actually worked at, say plainly that it was a working title if anyone asks, and let the bullets underneath do the confirming. Could changing my title get my offer rescinded? A genuine reframe almost never does; a fabrication genuinely can. Screeners sort discrepancies into two bins, the minor and explainable versus the material and misleading. A translated title backed by your real work and an offer letter lands in the first bin and gets waved through once you explain it. A promoted title you cannot defend lands in the second, and if it only surfaces after you have accepted and handed in your notice, it can pull the new job out from under you at the exact moment you have no fallback. Keep to the translation side of the line and this whole risk mostly disappears. Should I just keep my exact official title to be safe? If it is already clean and standard, absolutely leave it alone; nothing good comes from turning "Project Manager" into something with more syllables. Reframing only earns its keep when the real title is confusing, joke-y, or plainly undersells you. A handful of titles you cannot touch regardless, the credentialed ones such as Registered Nurse or CPA, because a license defines them rather than your preference. Stuck between options, default to your true official title paired with strong, specific bullets, a combination that stays honest, survives verification, and tends to persuade harder than any clever title swap could. title: CrowdStrike Global Enabling Tech Leader in Zero Trust Browser Security
summary: Frost & Sullivan named CrowdStrike the 2026 Global Enabling Technology Leader in Zero Trust Browser Security. Learn more.
body_text: Enforcing continuous in-session protection across any browser on managed and unmanaged devices establishes Falcon Secure Access as the new standard for browser security AUSTIN, Texas – July 1, 2026 – CrowdStrike (NASDAQ: CRWD) today announced it has been named Frost & Sullivan’s 2026 Global Enabling Technology Leader in Zero Trust Browser Security . The browser has become the operating environment for modern work, where employees access email, SaaS applications, collaboration tools, customer data, and AI services. All this activity makes the browser a high-value target for attackers – sitting between users, identities, applications, and sensitive enterprise data. Existing security models either force users into ‘walled garden’ enterprise browsers or rely on high-latency network routing. Powered by technology from CrowdStrike's acquisition of Seraphic , Falcon Secure Access defines a new model for secure access, enforcing protection directly within any browser runtime. This allows users to work in their browser of choice while eliminating the latency of network routing – turning any browser into a secure enterprise browser without forcing change or slowing productivity. “This disruptive model redefines browser security, and positions CrowdStrike as a catalyst for change in the global Zero Trust Browser Security market,” the report stated. "Forcing users into a dedicated browser or routing traffic through a proxy is not a security strategy; it's a tax on productivity," said Elia Zaitsev, chief technology officer, CrowdStrike. "By enforcing protection directly within any browser runtime, Falcon Secure Access delivers the flexibility the workforce demands and the security the business requires. This is browser security built for the modern enterprise." Combined with technology from CrowdStrike's acquisition of SGNL , Falcon Secure Access advances CrowdStrike's Next-Gen Identity Security strategy, creating a seamless security fabric that protects every interaction from the endpoint, through the browser session, and into the cloud. Key report findings include: Making Any Browser a Secure Enterprise Browser “CrowdStrike delivers unparalleled visibility and control across all browser types, including Chrome, Edge, Safari, Firefox, and emerging AI browsers.” A New Model for Security and Productivity “The cybersecurity industry has long grappled with the challenge of securing browser-based activity without degrading performance or user experience. Falcon Secure Access addresses this challenge through a groundbreaking innovation: a JavaScript runtime security module injected at the engine level, rather than relying on traditional browser extensions.” Securing Enterprise AI CrowdStrike secures how GenAI applications and agents are accessed through the browser, preventing shadow AI from scraping or exfiltrating sensitive data. Frost noted how the “ability to secure AI browsers and Electron apps (e.g., VS Code GPT integration) at the engine level addresses blind spots in traditional SASE/CASB models.” Security Wherever the Workforce Works CrowdStrike provides protection for contractors and third parties, and everywhere employees work: “Falcon Secure Access secures both managed and unmanaged devices, and supports mobile and desktop environments.” Unified Architecture CrowdStrike closes the gaps fragmented security stacks create: “Falcon Secure Access and the Falcon platform deliver on the company’s vision of stopping breaches by integrating with its Zero Trust Score, malware scanning, SaaS Security (SSPM), identity security, and SIEM telemetry.” To learn more about CrowdStrike’s recognition as Frost & Sullivan’s 2026 Global Enabling Technology Leader in Zero Trust Browser Security, visit here . About CrowdStrike CrowdStrike (NASDAQ: CRWD), a global cybersecurity leader, has redefined modern security with the world’s most advanced cloud-native platform for protecting critical areas of enterprise risk – endpoints and cloud workloads, identity and data. Powered by the CrowdStrike Security Cloud and world-class AI, the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform leverages real-time indicators of attack, threat intelligence, evolving adversary tradecraft, and enriched telemetry from across the enterprise to deliver hyper-accurate detections, automated protection and remediation, elite threat hunting, and prioritized observability of vulnerabilities. Purpose-built in the cloud with a single lightweight-agent architecture, the Falcon platform delivers rapid and scalable deployment, superior protection and performance, reduced complexity, and immediate time-to-value. title: My partner makes me feel crazy when I bring up a problem
summary: You raise something real and walk away doubting yourself. How to tell defensiveness from something that erodes your reality, and what helps.
body_text: You bring up something that bothered you. Ten minutes later you are the one apologizing, your original point has vanished, and you cannot even remember how you got here. You just know you feel a little unhinged, and they seem perfectly calm. If you have walked away from these conversations wondering whether you are the problem, that whiplash is worth paying attention to. The problem stops being the problem Here is the move, whether or not anyone is doing it on purpose. You raise issue A. Somehow the conversation becomes about your tone, your memory, how you always do this, why you are so sensitive. By the end you are defending your right to have brought it up at all, and issue A never got touched. Do that enough times and you start pre-editing yourself: rehearsing, softening, waiting for the perfect calm moment that never comes. That low hum of walking on eggshells is often the residue of exactly this pattern. Feeling crazy is not a character flaw. It is what happens when your read on reality keeps getting quietly overwritten. You remember the thing that happened. They tell you it did not happen that way, or did not happen at all, or happened because of something you did. Two accounts, and only one of you is allowed to be right. What people actually describe to us In Maia conversations, the tell is rarely one big dramatic fight. It is the small, repeated erosion. People say some version of: "I walked in sure of what I felt, and I walked out apologizing and I still don't totally know for what." They describe keeping notes on their phone so they can prove to themselves later that a conversation really did go the way they remember. They describe feeling most clear-headed when their partner is out of the house, and foggy again the moment they are back in the same room. When someone starts keeping evidence for their own sanity, that is usually the body noticing a pattern before the mind will let itself name it. Two things that look identical from the inside This part matters, because the fix is different for each. Feeling crazy after a hard conversation can come from two very different places. Reactive defensiveness. Your partner hears criticism, panics, and starts swinging: deflecting, changing the subject, bringing up your flaws. It is self-protective, not strategic. They are not trying to rewrite your reality, they are trying not to feel like a bad person for thirty seconds. When someone gets defensive every time you raise something , the conversation still derails, but there is usually remorse afterward, and they can hear you once the panic drops. Reality-eroding. The consistent effect, over time, is that you trust your own perception less. Your feelings get reframed as symptoms. "You're too sensitive." "That never happened." "You're remembering it wrong." The point of contact is not the original issue, it is your grip on what is true. This does not always come from cruelty, but the result is the same: you shrink, and they stay comfortable. The clumsy version tends to soften when things cool down. The eroding version tends to leave you more confused the more you engage, and weirdly responsible for a problem you did not create. How to stay standing in the conversation You cannot control whether they get defensive. You can hold onto your own reality, which is the thing that keeps getting knocked loose. Separate the fact from the feeling, and hold both. "On Tuesday you said you would call and you didn't. I felt dropped." The event happened. Your feeling is yours. Neither is up for a vote. Name the swerve out loud, gently. "We started on the missed call and now we're on my tone. Can we finish the first thing before we go there?" You are not accusing. You are refusing to let the topic get swapped. Do not defend your right to be upset. The second you argue about whether your feeling is valid, you have lost the thread. "I'm not going to debate whether I'm allowed to feel this. I'm telling you I do." Trust the version you had before the conversation scrambled it. If you keep needing proof for yourself, believe that instinct. It is data. If part of what stings is that you don't feel heard no matter how carefully you word things, that is worth naming as its own issue, not more evidence that you explained it wrong. When it stops being a communication problem Sometimes better technique genuinely helps, and a defensive partner who loves you will, over time, learn to stay in the room. But if you have tried every calm, fair, well-timed version and you still leave every conversation doubting your own mind, the issue may not be how you are bringing things up. It may be their willingness to let you be right about your own experience. A pattern where your reality is routinely rewritten, where you feel smaller and more confused over months, is not a wording problem. It is worth taking seriously, especially if it comes with control, fear, or feeling like you cannot leave. If any of that is present, talk to someone you trust, or reach the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233. Feeling like your feelings don't matter is not a small thing to keep absorbing. If you are trying to sort out which version you are actually in, that is a good thing to think through out loud with Maia. You can lay out what keeps happening, get help telling reactive defensiveness apart from something that keeps eroding your footing, and figure out what to try next for your specific situation, without anyone telling you that you are remembering it wrong.
